title: Spring Lecture #32: Master Spring Data JPA in one video

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes how `JpaRepository`, JPA and Hibernate relate to each other?
options: `JpaRepository` is defined by the Jakarta Persistence specification, and Hibernate implements it
Spring Data JPA replaces Hibernate, so `EntityManager` is no longer used underneath
Hibernate generates the `JpaRepository` implementation class at compile time
JPA is the specification, Hibernate is a JPA provider, and `JpaRepository` belongs to Spring Data JPA, which delegates to the `EntityManager`
questions.explanation: The notes stress that `JpaRepository` is part of Spring Data JPA, not the JPA specification. Spring Data creates a repository proxy at runtime whose standard methods (in `SimpleJpaRepository`) still delegate to the `EntityManager`, which is commonly implemented by Hibernate. Nothing is generated at compile time.

questions.question: Given this repository, which call returns the students whose name contains the text `har` anywhere in it?
options: `studentRepository.findByNameLike("har")`
`studentRepository.findByNameContaining("har")`
`studentRepository.findByName("%har%")`
`studentRepository.findByNameStartingWith("har")`
questions.explanation: With `Containing`, Spring Data wraps the value into a contains pattern (`%har%`) for you. With `Like`, the caller must supply the wildcards, so `"har"` without `%` matches only the exact value; `findByName` is a plain equality check, so `%` is not a wildcard there, and `StartingWith` matches only a prefix.

questions.question: This is the lecture's `fetchAll` method. The author expected the first two students ordered by name ascending, then age descending. What actually happens?
options: The two students are sorted by name then age, because the `Sort` object is picked up from the method's scope
It throws an exception, because a `Sort` was created but no sorted repository method was called
Two students are returned, but the `sort` is never passed, so the query has no ORDER BY and the order is not guaranteed; use `PageRequest.of(0, 2, sort)`
Every student is returned, because `findAll` ignores the page size when no sort is given
questions.explanation: The `Sort` object is built but never attached to the `Pageable`, so the generated query only limits to 2 rows. Without ORDER BY, the database does not guarantee any meaningful order. `PageRequest.of(page, size, sort)` combines both. (The `name` parameter is also unused.)

questions.question: A mobile app has an infinite-scroll student feed with a 'Load more' button; it never shows 'page 3 of 25'. Why is `Slice<Student> findByActiveTrue(Pageable pageable)` a better return type here than `Page<Student>`?
options: `Slice` doesn't need the total, so it avoids the extra COUNT query and typically just fetches one extra row to know `hasNext()`
`Slice` loads all matching rows once and caches them, so later pages need no queries
`Page` cannot be used with derived query methods, only with `findAll`
`Slice` sorts results automatically by id, while `Page` does not support sorting
questions.explanation: `Page` exposes `getTotalElements()` and `getTotalPages()`, which usually needs an additional count query that can be costly. `Slice` only knows whether another chunk exists, typically by requesting size + 1 rows. Both work with derived methods and both respect the `Sort` inside the `Pageable`.

questions.question: Inside a `@Transactional` service method you call `studentRepository.saveAndFlush(student)`, and later in the same method an exception causes a rollback. What happens to the INSERT that was flushed?
options: It stays in the database, because `saveAndFlush` commits the row immediately
It stays, because flushed statements cannot be undone by a rollback
It is never sent, because Hibernate always delays SQL until commit
It is rolled back: a flush only sends pending SQL to the database inside the transaction; it does not commit
questions.explanation: The notes state: flush = send pending SQL to the database; commit = permanently complete the transaction. After a flush the transaction can still roll back, undoing the INSERT. `saveAndFlush` is useful for detecting problems such as constraint violations early, not for committing early.

questions.question: The lecture's repository declares `@Query(value = "select * from student where email = :email", nativeQuery = true) Optional<Student> findByEmail(@Param("email") String email);`. A teammate deletes `nativeQuery = true` because "Spring Data can tell it's SQL". What happens?
options: Nothing changes; Spring Data detects `select *` and switches to native mode automatically
The string is now parsed as JPQL, where `select *` and raw table/column names are not valid, so the query is rejected as invalid
The query still runs, but returns `Object[]` rows instead of `Student` entities
Spring Data ignores the `@Query` and derives a query from the method name `findByEmail` instead
questions.explanation: Without `nativeQuery = true`, the `@Query` string is treated as JPQL, which works with entity names and fields (`SELECT s FROM Student s WHERE s.email = :email`). `select *` is SQL syntax, so the query fails validation. A declared `@Query` takes precedence over method-name derivation, so Spring Data does not quietly fall back to a derived query.

questions.question: A PUT endpoint calls the lecture's `updateStudent` method below. The service class has no `@Transactional` anywhere. The endpoint returns 200, but the row in the database is unchanged. Why?
options: `findById` runs in its own short repository transaction; the setters run after it has ended, and no later transaction flushes the change. Add `@Transactional` to the method (or call `save`)
Dirty checking only works on entities returned by `getReferenceById`, not `findById`
`Optional.get()` returns a copy of the entity, so changes never reach the managed instance
Setters generated by Lombok bypass Hibernate's change tracking; hand-written setters are required
questions.explanation: Dirty checking produces an UPDATE only when the persistence context is flushed, normally at commit of a transaction that covers the change. Here the only transaction is the one `SimpleJpaRepository.findById` opens, and it is already over when the setters run. Wrapping the method in `@Transactional` makes the entity managed for the whole method, so the UPDATE is generated at commit without calling `save()`.
questions.source: code: StudentService.updateStudent; notes p21-22 (save() versus dirty checking)

questions.question: The lecture repository declares `Optional<Student> findByEmailLike(String pattern);`. In production someone calls `findByEmailLike("%@gmail.com")` and 40 students match. What happens?
options: It returns `Optional.empty()`, because more than one row is treated as 'not found'
It returns an `Optional` holding the first matching row in id order
It throws an `IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException`, because a single-result return type got more than one row
It returns an `Optional` holding a `List<Student>` with all 40 rows
questions.explanation: An `Optional<Student>` (or plain `Student`) return type means a single-result query. When the query returns several rows, JPA raises a non-unique result error, which Spring translates to `IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException`. Use `List<Student>` for a pattern search, or `findFirst...OrderBy...` if one row is really wanted.

questions.question: `Student` has `@Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY) private Long id;` and no `@Version`. `detached` was loaded in an earlier request and has id 7, name "Rahul". What name is stored for student 7 after this method commits?
options: "Priya", because `save()` makes `detached` managed, so the later change is dirty-checked
"Aman", because `save()` merges the detached state and returns a different managed instance; `detached` itself stays detached
"Rahul", because `save()` on a non-new entity is a no-op
A duplicate row with a new id, because `save()` always issues an INSERT
questions.explanation: The id is non-null and there is no version property, so Spring Data treats the entity as not new and calls `merge()`. `merge()` copies the state (name "Aman") onto a managed instance and returns it; the argument does not become managed, so the later `setName("Priya")` is not tracked. That is why the notes say the return value of `save()` matters for detached entities.

questions.question: `GET /students?page=N&size=10` uses `PageRequest.of(page, 10, Sort.by("name"))`. Many students share the same name, and users report that some students appear on two pages while others never appear. What is the recommended fix?
options: Switch from `Page` to `Slice`, because the count query is shifting the offsets
Increase the page size so duplicates fall onto the same page
Sort with `Sort.Direction.DESC` instead of ascending
Add a unique tie-breaker so the order is deterministic, e.g. `Sort.by("name").ascending().and(Sort.by("id").ascending())`
questions.explanation: Page boundaries depend on ordering. When the sort key is not unique, rows with equal names can be returned in a different order on each request, so OFFSET-based pages overlap or skip rows. Adding a unique tie-breaker like `id` makes the order stable; changing the direction, page size or using `Slice` does not remove the ambiguity.
questions.source: notes p39-40 (Sorting and pagination must work together)
